summary:
Visitors in Gombe State stand under two overlapping criminal regimes. Nationally, the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reaches all persons including tourists, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex conduct, cohabitation between same-sex partners, public shows of a same-sex relationship and the operation of gay organisations; the UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025, updated April 2026) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.

Gombe is one of the twelve northern states that had adopted Shari'a into its criminal legislation by 2002, as documented in Human Rights Watch's 2004 report, with Shari'a courts holding criminal jurisdiction over Muslims beyond federal law. The state's Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001 was signed on 23 November 2001 and criminalises same-sex conduct by men and women beyond the federal code.

The statutory penalties in Gombe are severe. Unmarried men convicted of sodomy face caning of 100 lashes plus one year's imprisonment; married men face stoning to death (rajm). The lesbianism offence carries up to 50 lashes plus imprisonment of up to six months. Gombe defines gross indecency in its own formulation as any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour, a formulation broad enough to reach gender non-conformity as well as sex acts.

The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records that Islamic law applies to Muslims in the twelve northern states and criminalises same-sex sexual acts both between men and between women; the maximum penalty for sodomy for men is death in all twelve states, and penalties for lesbianism range from death to flogging and imprisonment. That note carries a dedicated section on enforcement of Shari'a provisions and the attitude of the hisbah, the morality police. Whether the Shari'a layer formally reaches non-Muslim visitors is not settled by these sources; its practical reach is mediated by arrest practice and morality policing rather than by any exemption for tourists.

Enforcement in Gombe is documented at incident level. In October 2023 the Gombe State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps raided a gathering at Duwa Plaza along the Bauchi-Gombe Expressway that was preparing a same-sex wedding, arresting 76 people. State PRO Buhari Sa'ad told reporters that 59 males were detained, 21 of whom wilfully confessed to being homosexuals, with 17 females present, and that they would be charged to court for a crime of social vice in Gombe State. The Guardian of 23 October 2023 independently confirmed the arrests through Gombe NSCDC Commandant Mohammed Muazu and spokesperson Buhari Saad, who said the remaining males and the 17 females were invited guests and onlookers, and noted officers' concern over the participants' ages.

No trans-specific incident or documented hisbah activity appears in the sources assembled for Gombe. Trans identity is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed: Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here. Absence of records reflects fear of outing and surveillance gaps rather than absence of risk.
tangentialFactors:
Gombe's sodomy and lesbianism penalties are shared verbatim with Jigawa, Kano and Zamfara, indicating a common statutory template across much of the twelve-state Shari'a bloc rather than a Gombe-specific measure. The federal SSMPA applies nationwide on top of that template, so conduct lawful in southern states carries the same national exposure here, with the additional state penalties.

The October 2023 Gombe raid is corroborated by two independent outlets, Sahara Reporters and the Lagos-based Guardian, which strengthens it as evidence of active enforcement rather than a single-source claim. The scale of the operation, involving 76 arrests from a tip-off about a private birthday gathering, indicates that surveillance reaches private social events and not only public conduct.

Police and security violence against perceived gay people is a documented feature of the wider national environment: TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports a man stopped by Lagos police struck with a gun butt and released after paying part of a 50,000 naira bribe for looking gay, and the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs luring LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing. Dating-app use carries that risk in Gombe as elsewhere in Nigeria.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Shari'a law in northern states. Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the SSMPA reinforced colonial-era criminalisation.

The Shari'a layer in Gombe applies to Muslims, and Shari'a courts hold criminal jurisdiction over them beyond federal law. Residents therefore face a dual exposure: the federal SSMPA and the state Shari'a Penal Code Law 2001, with the state offences covering same-sex conduct by women as well as men, which the federal statute does not reach in the same terms.

The enacted statutory text punishes unmarried men convicted of sodomy with 100 lashes and one year's imprisonment, and married men with stoning to death. Lesbianism carries up to 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment. Gombe's own definition of gross indecency, any sexual offence against the normal or usual standards of behaviour, gives prosecutors a broad local charge independent of the SSMPA.

Arrest practice is a live factor for residents. The October 2023 NSCDC operation resulted in 76 detentions, with 21 of the 59 detained males recorded as having confessed, and state authorities stated the detainees would be charged in court. Morality policing through the hisbah is a documented feature of enforcement across the twelve-state bloc, and the UK Home Office note treats hisbah attitude as a distinct enforcement variable.

Trans residents have no explicit statutory protection and no explicit statutory recognition. Placement questions in custody are resolved by official discretion: in the Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye) case, sentenced on 12 April 2024 to six months for naira abuse and held in a maximum-security prison in Lagos, press coverage openly asked which prison the authorities would keep her in, and an October 2024 investigative panel found that housing her in a maximum-security facility violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted is unresolved in the sources available here; no Gombe-specific instrument on cross-dressing is documented.

No trans-specific killing, arrest or complaint in Gombe appears in this inventory. The nearest national reference point is the August 2024 killing of the 33-year-old transgender TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, whose beaten body was found on a highway in Abuja and for whom The Dial (February 2025) recorded that no suspects had been charged six months later; whether comparable incidents occurred in Gombe is not sourced.

Hisbah activity is documented as a general feature of the twelve-state bloc, including through the UK Home Office's dedicated enforcement section, but no named hisbah intervention in Gombe is recorded in these sources. The practical reach of the Shari'a layer over non-Muslim visitors is likewise not resolved by the inventory.

Charging decisions in the October 2023 Gombe case are stated as intentions by state spokespersons; the sources do not record the court outcome, sentences imposed, or whether any of the 76 detainees were convicted.

Reporting-decay caveat: absence of records for Gombe reflects fear of outing and surveillance gaps rather than absence of risk, and the inventory carries no source dated after the October 2023 raid for this state.
